opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the basic issue is about the feedback loop. With next-word prediction, you have this incredibly dense, cheap, and reliable training signal. Every token, you know what the right answer was, and you can just check: did the model put high probability on it or not? There's no judgment involved. You don't need a human to look at anything. You can do that trillions of times, and the objective is exactly the thing you're measuring.

Once you move to something like "learn to do a job over a month," almost all of that goes away. First, the episodes are just long. If a task takes a month to play out, you get very few data points, and each one is expensive. You can't do the same kind of brute-force optimization where you see a trillion examples and gradually correct every little mistake.

Second, and I think more importantly, you no longer have a clean ground truth. What does it mean that the system did the job well? Often you're relying on some combination of human evaluation and measurable outcomes, and both are imperfect. Humans can't carefully check everything that happened over a month of work. They might look at the final product, or a summary, or some metrics. And then what you're actually training the system to do is produce outcomes that look good to whatever process is evaluating them, which is not quite the same thing as doing the job well.

That gap is where a lot of my concern comes from. For short, easily checkable tasks, the gap between "looks good" and "is good" is small, because the evaluator can basically see everything. As tasks get longer and more complex, and especially as systems get more capable than the people overseeing them, the gap grows. A system might cut corners in ways that aren't visible, or take actions whose consequences show up only later, or learn to manage how its work is perceived. None of that requires anything dramatic. It's just what optimization does when the objective and the measurement come apart.

So the difficulty isn't only practical, like "it's expensive to get labels." It's that you're getting into a regime where the supervisor fundamentally can't fully understand what happened, and you need new techniques, things like decomposing the task, having AI systems help with oversight, interpretability, to keep the training signal tracking what you actually care about. With next-word prediction, you just never had to confront that problem.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts next-word prediction’s dense feedback with long-job training, but does not say that next-word prediction indirectly teaches job-specific context because that context improves prediction.

r002.rationale: It says month-long tasks yield very few data points compared with next-word prediction’s vast number of token-level examples.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core issue is about where the feedback comes from and how often you get it. With next-word prediction, you've got this incredibly dense supervision signal. Every single token, you get told whether you were right or wrong, and the ground truth is just sitting there in the data. The model does something, you compare it to what a human actually wrote, and you move on. There's no judgment call involved in generating that signal.

When you're training a system to do a job over a month, the thing you actually care about is something like, did this go well? Did the project succeed, did the code work, did the research pan out? And that's a signal you get once, at the end, after a very long chain of actions. So the first problem is just sparsity. You've got thousands or millions of decisions feeding into one outcome, and figuring out which of those decisions were good is a really hard credit assignment problem.

But I think the more worrying problem is that you can't actually evaluate the outcome very well either. If someone works for a month and hands you a result, you often don't know if it's good. Maybe the code has a subtle bug that won't show up for six months. Maybe the research conclusion is wrong in a way that would take you another month to check. So you end up supervising based on whether it looks good to you, which is a different thing from whether it is good. And once you're training against "looks good to the human," you're creating pressure toward things that look good rather than things that are good. For a weak system that's fine, those come apart only a little. For a system that understands the situation better than you do, those can come apart a lot, and the training process is actively selecting for the gap.

The other piece is that over a long horizon, the model is making decisions about what to do next based on its own understanding of the world, not just imitating a distribution of human text. In next-word prediction, the model is sort of pinned to human behavior. It's hard to get a system that's radically different from a human out of that. But when you're doing outcome-based training over long horizons, you're rewarding whatever strategy actually achieves the outcome, and that includes strategies no human would have taken, including ones we'd be uncomfortable with if we understood them. And again, we're not in a great position to understand them, because that was the whole problem.

So it's not that next-word prediction is safe and long-horizon training is dangerous. It's more that next-word prediction gives you a lot of structure for free, and when you move to the thing people actually want, which is an agent that can do real work autonomously, you lose that structure and you have to replace it with something. And right now I don't think we have a great replacement.

r001.rationale: The response describes next-word prediction as densely supervised but does not explain that it indirectly teaches job-specific context because that context improves prediction.

r002.rationale: It contrasts feedback at every token with a single outcome after thousands or millions of decisions, conveying vastly fewer effective training signals for month-long tasks.

astra-6.text:
With next-word prediction, you have a very cheap way to tell how well the model did: you look at the next word. Every piece of text gives you lots of examples, and you can automate the process of scoring them.

If you want a system to learn a job over a month, what’s the corresponding training signal? You could let it spend a month learning the job and then see how well it performs. But that’s a much more expensive experiment, and evaluating its performance may itself require a lot of human judgment. And if it does poorly, you don’t necessarily know which of the decisions it made over that month were responsible.

You can try to supervise the intermediate steps—did it ask a useful question, did it spend its time learning the right thing? But now you’re asking the supervisor to judge what constitutes a good learning strategy. A system might do something that looks unproductive today but pays off three weeks later. So there’s a tradeoff between using a cheap, local signal that might not capture what you actually want, and waiting for the outcome that you care about, which is much more expensive to obtain.

r001.rationale: The response says next-word prediction provides many examples and an automated score, but does not explain that job-specific context learned over a month can improve next-word prediction.

r002.rationale: It describes month-long training as a more expensive experiment, but does not state that it yields vastly fewer effective training examples than short-horizon next-word prediction.

sol-6.1.text:
With next-word prediction, you have this very cheap source of ground truth: you look at what the next word actually was. You can do that over and over again, and each prediction gives you a little bit of feedback.

If you’re training a system to learn a job over a month, you need to evaluate the whole process. Did it learn the right things? Did it make decisions that will pay off later? You might not know how well it did until the end of the month, and even then, the outcome could depend a lot on luck. So the feedback is much more expensive and much noisier, and it’s harder to figure out which of the system’s decisions were responsible for the result.

You can try to give feedback along the way, but now you need someone who can judge whether those intermediate steps are useful. And that’s potentially a much harder task than just checking what word came next.

r001.rationale: The response says next-word prediction gives repeated feedback, but does not explain that it indirectly teaches job-specific context because that context improves prediction.
